title: One good analogy
summary: Explain binary to a grandparent using one everyday analogy, judged by whether they can say it back in their own words.
materials: a grandparent or grown-up with ten minutes to spare

steps.title: What makes an analogy good
steps.body:
An analogy is a bridge. It carries something the listener already knows across to the thing they do not know yet. This week you built binary with your own hands, and today you carry it to someone who has never seen a bit in their life.

Three rules for a strong bridge. First, start from something your listener touches every day: light switches in the house, coins in a purse, fingers on a hand. Second, match the part that matters. Binary's heart is two states, on and off, and places that double in worth, so your analogy must carry that part, not just say computers are like magic. Compare these two: binary is like a secret code says almost nothing, but each finger is a light switch, and the switches are worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 carries the whole machine across. Third, be honest about where the bridge ends. Every analogy breaks somewhere, and saying where it breaks makes people trust the rest of it more.

The test of your analogy is not whether it sounds clever. It is whether your listener can say it back to you in their own words and get it right. That is the whole judging rule today.

The question of the week: is zero something or nothing? On your fingers, zero is a closed fist, no fingers up at all, and yet that fist still tells you a number. Keep the question in your head while you practice, and end your recording with your answer.

steps.title: Build the analogy and test it
steps.body:
Pick your person: a grandparent is perfect, any grown-up who does not know binary works too. Pick their everyday thing, something they know better than you do.

Write your analogy in three sentences. Sentence one: the thing they know. Sentence two: how counting with on and off works just like it, including why the places are worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Sentence three: one place where the analogy stops being true.

Practice it once out loud, alone, with a timer. Then do it for real: tell them the analogy, let them ask one question, and then ask them to explain it back to you in their own words. Listen without interrupting. If their version comes back wrong, that is not their mistake, it is the bridge's, so fix the analogy and try the new version.
checklist: My analogy uses something my listener already knows well
It carries the part that matters: two states, and places that double
I can name one place where the analogy breaks
My listener said it back in their own words, and the important part survived

steps.title: The two chair debate
steps.body:
The motion: machines understand numbers better than people do. You argued games with Rebut last season. Today you play both sides yourself.

Set out two chairs. In chair one, argue for the motion for two minutes: think about what your four LEDs never get wrong, how fast they are, how they never get bored. In chair two, argue against it for two minutes: think about who decided what the lights mean, who wired the places, and whether the LEDs know they are counting at all.

The steelman rule applies to both chairs: before you answer a point from the other chair, say that point back as fairly and strongly as you can. A grown-up listens and, at the end, asks one hard question of each chair. Then step out of both chairs and say which one you actually believe today, and why.
checklist: I gave the strongest case I could from both chairs, not just my favourite side
Before answering a point, I said the other chair's point back fairly
Each chair used one real example from my own binary display
I ended by saying which chair I believe today, and gave my reason

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the analogy telling: you explain binary with your analogy, then your listener says it back in their own words. Close the recording with your answer to the question of the week: is zero something or nothing?
